name: Greedy Algorithms and When They Fail
intent: Recognise the problems where picking the best-looking option at each step is provably optimal (interval scheduling by earliest finish), spot the ones where it is not (coin change with odd denominations, weighted jobs, 0/1 knapsack), and use greedy deliberately as a fast heuristic when you know what it costs.
scenario: A scheduler must fit as many of 1,000 jobs as possible into one room. Sorting by earliest finish time gives 241 jobs and is provably the best; sorting by earliest start gives 153 and sorting by shortest job gives 237, which look sensible and are wrong. Then the jobs get weights, and the same earliest-finish rule collects 2,460 where 3,084 was possible. A coin-change routine that works for the familiar 1, 5, 10, 25 returns too many coins for 1, 3, 4.
problem: A greedy algorithm builds an answer one irrevocable choice at a time, always taking the option that looks best right now. When it works it is short, fast and hard to beat. When it does not, it returns a wrong answer without any error, and it usually passes every test you thought of, because the coin sets and inputs people try first are the friendly ones. The skill is knowing which problems have the structure that makes greedy safe, and having a way to check, rather than trusting that a rule feels natural.

howItWorks.title: The shape of a greedy algorithm
howItWorks.text: Order the candidates by some rule, then walk through them once and keep each one that is still allowed. There is no backtracking: a choice made is final. That is why greedy is cheap: after the sort, one pass. For 1,000 jobs it takes 9,730 comparisons and checks. Everything depends on the rule, and 'earliest', 'biggest' and 'shortest' all sound reasonable while giving different answers.

howItWorks.title: When it is right: interval scheduling by earliest finish
howItWorks.text: To schedule the most non-overlapping jobs, always take the job that finishes first among those still free. This is optimal: with 1,000 jobs it picks 241, and nothing does better. Two other natural rules lose: earliest start picks 153, because one long job that starts first blocks many short ones, and shortest first picks 237, because a short job sitting between two others can block both. A brute-force check over every subset of 14 jobs finds a best of 3 where those two rules reach only 2, a useful habit for testing a rule on tiny inputs.

howItWorks.title: Why it is right: the exchange argument in plain words
howItWorks.text: Take any best schedule. Its first job finishes no earlier than the greedy job, because greedy picked the earliest finish. Swap that first job for the greedy one: the greedy job ends no later, so it cannot collide with anything after it, and the schedule is just as large. So some best schedule begins with greedy's choice. Remove that job and every job it overlaps, and repeat the same argument on what is left. If you cannot tell such a story for your rule ('whatever the best answer does, I can change it to use my choice without making it worse'), you have no reason to believe the rule.

howItWorks.title: When it breaks: odd denominations and weights
howItWorks.text: With coins 1, 3 and 4 and amount 6, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins) while 3 + 3 (2 coins) is better; over the amounts 1 to 1,000 it is wrong for 249 of them. With 1, 5, 10, 25 it is never wrong in that range, and with 1, 5, 10, 20, 25 it first fails at 40 (25 + 10 + 5 against 20 + 20). Adding weights to the jobs breaks earliest-finish too: 2,460 total weight against an optimum of 3,084, and 'heaviest first' only gets 2,689. The failure is the same each time: a locally best choice closes off a better combination, and the rule never looks back.

howItWorks.title: Use it on purpose: the price of the optimum, and greedy as a heuristic
howItWorks.text: The alternative to a greedy rule is usually dynamic programming, which tries both choices and remembers the results. It is exact and costs more: for 100,000 with coins 1, 5, 10, 25, greedy needs 4 steps and the table method 400,000. Sometimes close is good enough. For 0/1 knapsack, taking items by value per weight reached 1,256 against an optimum of 1,263 at 80 items, but 80 against 89 at 10 items, and nothing guarantees it. Know which case you are in: provably optimal, approximate with a proven bound (greedy set cover is within about a factor of ln n of the best possible), or just a heuristic you have measured.

pros: Short, fast and easy to implement: usually a sort and one pass, so n log n overall
When the problem has the right structure (interval scheduling, minimum spanning trees, Huffman codes) it is exactly optimal, with a clear proof
A good baseline and a good starting point for a more careful search
Easy to reason about what it did and why
cons: Wrong without warning when the structure is missing, and ordinary tests rarely show it
A greedy answer has no certificate of quality unless you have a proof or an approximation bound
The 'obvious' rule is often not the right one: several plausible rules give different answers on the same input
It never reconsiders, so one early mistake cannot be repaired
whenToUse: You can state an exchange argument or a known theorem that covers your problem (earliest finish for intervals, Kruskal or Prim for spanning trees, Huffman for prefix codes)
A quick approximate answer is acceptable and you have measured how far it is from the optimum on realistic inputs
You need a starting solution for an iterative improvement method
The inputs are of a known friendly shape, such as a fixed coin system that has been checked
whenNotToUse: The problem has weights or values that interact with capacity or conflicts (weighted intervals, 0/1 knapsack, arbitrary coin sets) and you need the exact optimum
Denominations, costs or rules are configurable by users: a set that was safe today is not safe after someone adds a coin
The cost of a wrong answer is high and nobody can write down why the rule is optimal
A decision early on makes later ones impossible, with no way to undo it: that calls for search or dynamic programming
pitfalls: Testing greedy only on the familiar coin set 1, 5, 10, 25: it passes 1,000 of 1,000 amounts, so the bug in 1, 3, 4 (wrong for 249 of 1,000) never shows up until the coins change
Picking a rule because it sounds natural: earliest start gives 153 jobs and shortest first 237 against the optimal 241 from the same data. Natural is not a proof
Reusing a rule that is optimal for one goal after the goal changes: earliest finish is optimal for counting jobs and loses 20% of the weight once jobs have values (2,460 against 3,084)
Treating a heuristic's result as the optimum: 1,256 against 1,263 looks fine and 80 against 89 does not. Compare against an exact method on small inputs to learn the typical gap
Forgetting tie-breaks: when two candidates have the same key, the order can change the answer; make the tie-break part of the rule and keep it stable
Assuming Dijkstra-style greedy works with negative edges: the shortest-path greedy needs non-negative weights, and a negative edge can make an already finalised node wrong
Skipping the cheap sanity check: for small inputs, enumerate every subset (2 to the power 14 is 16,384) and compare. If it disagrees once, the rule is not an algorithm, it is a guess

roles.label: Candidates
roles.description: The jobs, coins or items the algorithm chooses among.

roles.label: Greedy rule
roles.description: The ordering that decides which candidate looks best right now.

roles.label: Solution so far
roles.description: The choices already made; none of them is ever taken back.

roles.label: Exact method
roles.description: A search or table that tries all the options, used to check or replace greedy.

quiz.question: Why is 'take the job that finishes earliest' optimal for scheduling the most non-overlapping jobs?
options: Short jobs are always better, so the one finishing first is the shortest.
It examines all subsets of jobs in a clever order and keeps the largest one.
Any best schedule can swap its first job for this one without losing a job or causing an overlap.
Sorting by finish time is the cheapest sort, so the result is cheapest too.
quiz.explanation: The earliest-finishing job ends no later than any other first job, so swapping it in cannot collide with the rest. Repeating that on what remains shows the greedy schedule is as large as the best one. A job that finishes first need not be short.

quiz.question: Greedy needs 4 steps for 100,000 with coins 1, 5, 10, 25 and a table needs 400,000. What should that cost difference make you conclude?
options: Greedy is always the right choice, because cheaper means better.
The table method is needed for every amount over 1,000.
Greedy and the table agree for any coin set, so only speed matters.
Greedy is only safe for coin sets known or tested to suit it; for 1, 3, 4 it is wrong for 249 of the first 1,000 amounts.
quiz.explanation: Cost and correctness are separate questions. The price of the table method buys a guarantee that greedy lacks for odd coin sets. The familiar set is safe to use greedily; one added or changed coin can break that.

quiz.question: Greedy by value per weight reaches 1,256 against an optimum of 1,263 for 80 knapsack items, but 80 against 89 for 10 items. What does it show?
options: The algorithm has a bug that appears only with few items.
It is a heuristic: often close, with no guarantee, so measure the gap against an exact method.
Greedy improves by a fixed percentage with every extra item.
The table method is wrong for small inputs and greedy is right.
quiz.explanation: With whole items, a greedy fill can leave unused capacity that a different combination would use. The loss is small relative to a big total and large relative to a small one. Check against an exact method on small inputs to learn the typical gap.
